title: Why decision-making is key to effective cyber resilience | World Economic Forum
author: SM
text: Cyber resilience is now inseparable from economic resilience and is essential for digital trust, economic competitiveness and societal stability. Here's how a cyber resilience decision system framework can enhance an organization's abilities to make informed decisions amid evolving cyber threats.As enterprises increasingly depend on cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to expand their global digital footprint, the impact of cybersecurity attacks is no longer restricted to just enterprise-level operations. Geopolitical fragmentation and a proliferation of sophisticated cyber threats are now exposing critical security gaps in digital ecosystems across the world.The World Economic Forum’s Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026 reflects this broader shift, showing that cyber resilience has now become inseparable from economic resilience, while highlighting its importance in facilitating digital trust, economic competitiveness and societal stability.The Global Cybersecurity Outlook also observes a paradox that is consistently surfacing. Different organizations with similar threats, investments in cybersecurity and governance frameworks achieve different resilience outcomes. While some recover swiftly from disruptions caused by cyber threats, others experience prolonged operational, financial and reputational consequences.The question has changed from whether organizations understand cybersecurity threats to why organizations with the same levels of awareness and visibility into cyber threats make different resilience decisions and achieve varied outcomes.The cyber resilience paradox in practiceTo bring this paradox into focus, let’s explore two different cyber crises and their outcomes.In February 2024, US-based Change Healthcare experienced a ransomware attack that disrupted care for several weeks. This severely affected several healthcare providers that relied heavily on a single digital platform for their operations. However, nationwide healthcare providers that followed different operating procedures, relied on manual workarounds and had clearly defined executive decision-making processes were far less impacted.The biggest threats to cybersecurity today, according to 5 experts03:29Later that year, the global CrowdStrike outage highlighted the same lesson on a larger scale, as thousands of organizations, including airlines, banks and hospitals, went offline and only had access to limited information.Many faced several days of disruption that affected customers, employees and essential services, but others were able to restore critical services within hours due to predefined recovery processes guided by a clear decision-making authority.In both cases, it was clear that visibility into the problem was not the concern, but rather the lack of a response model that enabled timely, coordinated action.Why organizations should look beyond visibilityVisibility into cyber threats and the execution of remedial actions are critical factors in defining cybersecurity resilience. Today, organizations have unprecedented visibility with the help of threat intelligence, monitoring platforms and risk quantification tools.Governance has matured through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 in the US, the ISO 27001 international standard for information security management systems and the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, resulting in stronger accountability, improved oversight and elevated cyber resilience. Incident response and business continuity capabilities continue to become more sophisticated as well.Have you read?Why the satellite communications boom needs stronger cyber resilienceArticleHow companies can quantify cyber resilience – and why it’s important they doArticleWhile these advancements have transformed cybersecurity into a mature business discipline, they have also exposed new constraints. Visibility does not determine which risks organizations need to mitigate, transfer or accept.A governance framework guides organizations in mitigating risks but does not help top management prioritize resilience investments, which depend on business objectives, financial constraints, risk appetite and strategic priorities. Dashboards can help security teams identify and understand existing risks but do not help determine where scarce resources will deliver resilience benefits.Building a cyber resilience decision system frameworkExisting cybersecurity frameworks improve visibility, governance and accountability, but often leave organizations to figure out where to invest limited resources across competing resilience priorities. This creates a missing decision layer in cyber resilience.To address this gap, organizations need to move toward adopting a decision architecture that can continuously translate visibility into optimized action. One such architecture is the cyber resilience decision system (CRDS) framework, which integrates cyber visibility, business priorities, financial considerations, ecosystem dependencies and operational execution into a continuous decision capability.The CRDS framework improves the quality, consistency and transparency of decisions made under uncertainty. By integrating the following four core capabilities, CRDS offers organizations a framework to improve resilience outcomes:Identity trust: Establishes trust between humans and AI, as both are integral participants in the digital economy.Economic alignment: Includes cyber risk in economic decision-making, helping leaders assess resilience investments based on business value and not technical severity.Ecosystem assessment: Evaluates ecosystem resilience by mapping cloud providers, software vendors, and critical infrastructure operators in a deeply connected digital ecosystem.Decision-ready intelligence: Transforms technical cyber intelligence into clear options that help executives understand trade-offs, prioritize investments and align cyber resilience with broader business strategy.Putting the CRDS framework into practiceLet’s look at a hypothetical scenario. A security scan discovers an exploitable vulnerability in multiple business-critical applications. Standard cybersecurity frameworks can identify affected systems and assess the impact, but may offer limited guidance on where to prioritize remediation.The cyber resilience decision system fills the gap. It takes a broad view of risk and prioritizes remediation based on an application’s criticality to business function, its impact on business-as-usual (BAU) operations, and its overall impact on the business. To use CRDS, an organization should be able to:Identify and prioritize all applications based on how critical the application is to business function.Map these applications to the BAU operations they support, and rank those operations by impact.Remediate vulnerabilities according to the sequence established by the CRDS model.CRDS helps C-suite executives prioritize remediation backlogs, while balancing security requirements, business continuity and organizational goals.By guiding decisions on where to act, what to prioritize and how to allocate resources, this approach can help reduce mean time to recover and improve organizational resilience.In conclusion, the CRDS framework represents the next frontier for modern cyber resilience, as it goes beyond the ability to withstand an attack to the capability to make informed decisions in the face of evolving cyber threats.For cybersecurity leaders, these decisions include where to act, what to prioritize and how much to invest. The real measure of cyber resilience is how effectively organizations turn what they know into timely, coordinated action.Follow this topic. Create a free account for personalized updates.
